Embora inicialmente se acreditasse que botar ovos com casca dura fosse crucial para o sucesso evolutivo das espécies amniotas, incluindo mamíferos, lagartos, crocodilianos e pássaros, novas pesquisas sugerem uma visão mais ampla. Pesquisadores da Universidade de Bristol e da Universidade de Nanjing descobriram que algumas espécies que botam ovos podem ter evoluído de ancestrais vivíparos, desafiando as suposições anteriores.

Essas descobertas redefinem nossa compreensão sobre a evolução da reprodução animal, mostrando que a capacidade de botar ovos com casca dura pode não ter sido tão precoce ou tão fundamental quanto se pensava. A diversidade de modos reprodutivos, incluindo a retenção prolongada de embriões, desempenhou um papel importante no sucesso evolutivo das espécies. Portanto, a galinha veio antes do ovo, marcando uma reviravolta intrigante na narrativa evolutiva.

O que você achou dessa curiosidade?

As verdadeiras frutas do morango, no ponto de vista da botânica, são aqueles pontinhos pretos, que muita gente pensa que são sementes, sabe? Esses pontinhos são chamados de aquênios. Cada um deles é uma frutinha com uma sementinha dentro.

Que o Monte Everest é a montanha mais alta do planeta Terra todo mundo já sabe, mas você sabia que a colisão que o formou continua acontecendo até hoje? Não? 👀 Então vem cá!

O Monte Everest foi formado devido a uma colisão tectônica entre a placa indiana e a placa da Eurásia há dezenas de milhões de anos, e segundo pesquisas, a Índia se desloca em direção ao norte alguns centímetros por ano. Os cientistas calculam que o impacto ainda em rumo à Eurásia pode levar as montanhas a ficarem cada vez mais altas, com um crescimento médio esperado de aproximadamente 10 milímetros por ano na porção noroeste da cordilheira, e cerca de um milímetro por ano no Everest. 🗻

Mesmo com a erosão e a gravidade preservando as condições das montanhas imponentes, as placas tectônicas mantêm sua dança geológica, e o Everest continuará acompanhando seus passos. Tornando-se, então, uma área tectonicamente ativa e instável. Aos alpinistas, cuidado: é muito interessante, mas igualmente ordinário. #MUITOinteressante #monteeverest

Um grupo de pesquisadores dos Estados Unidos descobriu que pequenas quantidades de álcool podem reduzir o estresse no cérebro, beneficiando a saúde cardiovascular. 😊

🚨Mas cuidado: isso não significa que você deve beber para prevenir doenças cardíacas ou derrames. O álcool também aumenta o risco de câncer em qualquer quantidade de consumo.

O estudo analisou mais de 50 mil pessoas que participaram de um banco de dados que reúne informações genéticas, clínicas, de estilo de vida e socioeconômicas de pacientes voluntários.

Os pesquisadores encontraram uma associação entre o consumo leve a moderado de álcool e uma menor incidência de eventos cardiovasculares, como infartos e derrames, mesmo após ajustar para outros fatores de risco.

Além disso, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens cerebrais de centenas desses pacientes e observaram que aqueles que bebiam de forma leve a moderada tinham menores respostas ao estresse na amígdala, a parte do cérebro que processa o medo e as ameaças.

Essa redução na atividade cerebral relacionada ao estresse parece explicar em grande parte a proteção cardiovascular observada nos bebedores leves a moderados.

Se rosa for a sua cor favorita, você precisa saber que ela não passa de uma ilusão criada pelo nosso cérebro quando vê duas cores opostas se misturando: o vermelho e o violeta.

Essas são as cores que estão nas pontas do arco-íris, e elas não formam uma nova cor de luz, mas sim uma nova cor de pigmento. O pigmento é a substância que dá cor às coisas, como as tintas, os lápis de cor e os gizes de cera.

Então, quando nós vemos algo rosa, na verdade nós estamos vendo algo que tem pigmentos vermelhos e violetas misturados. Os nossos olhos recebem essas duas cores e mandam para o nosso cérebro. O nosso cérebro então cria a sensação de rosa, que é algo intermediário entre o vermelho e o violeta. Mas essa cor só existe na nossa mente, não na luz.

Por isso que o rosa não existe do mesmo jeito que as outras cores. Ela é uma ilusão criada pela nossa cabeça, mas isso não significa que ela seja menos importante ou bonita do que as outras cores. Ela é apenas diferente, e isso é legal. Você pode usar a cor rosa para pintar muitas coisas legais, como flores, animais, roupas e até bonecas!!

I was surprised how many people responded to what I wrote yesterday and glad to know people found comfort in my thoughts. 🙏 Often this feeling of being “lost” comes from a larger cultural context. I just got back from Bhutan, a place where life feels integrated, whole, directed. One of my favorite homes is Hawaii. 🏝Tomorrow I’m going there.🤙Part of why I love Hawaii and why it feels like home to me is similar to the feeling I get in Bhutan. Rinpung Monastery, Paro, Bhutan. A “dzong” is the word they use  in Bhutan for a fortress/monastery. These beautiful structures with giant walls reveal a lot about Bhutan’s unique culture. First, it is a defensible fortress--a holdover from days when wars were still happening. You can’t see from the picture I took here, but the walls descend further, so there’s no way for attackers to climb up or get inside. There’s tiny slits  around the Dzong where people inside can shoot arrows at attackers on the outside! 🏹I’ve seen 10 fortresses like this in throughout Bhutan, and they’re usually built on a hillside with a strategic view of the valley, and, if the view isn’t so great, there’s a secondary watchtower in a better position. But what are they defending? I am just learning, but there’s a unique confluence of activity inside each Dzong: besides a military fortress, today, Dzong’s are homes for monks, and a spiritual center, but they also house all kinds of offices—think of it like the combination church, DMV, a civil court, an architecture planning office, and anything else related to the city’s administration. It shows how there is a lack of separation between “church and state”… In Bhutan, their philosophical and “religious” beliefs (some say Buddhism is not a religion, but a philosophical perspective), are integrated with the government, not separated. 🎊More Bhutanese are beginning to dress like Westerners, but when you visit the Dzong, you are required to where the traditional dress of the Bhutanese people. To foreign eyes, it makes for a colorful and exciting experience—you feel like you’re in the 16th century watching the activity inside, even though people might be there to get architectural plans approved, or to get a divorce, or something else that seems very “modern” to us. Ah yes, and the chilis… I had to include the chilis drying in the sun. Bhutanese add chilis to almost every dish (even in their rice); certainly there will be chilis in every meal! The chilis are dried outside, typically on the roof of homes. 🏠 Drying can take a month! ☀️I think I’ll be adding chilis to dishes when i get back home! 😀

Tiger’s Nest, Bhutan. 🇧🇹 When I first told people I was planning a trip to Bhutan, very few knew what I was talking about. 🤔Where? What? For those that did know Bhutan, it was always for one of two things: 1) the pleasant idea that the government and King make policy decisions based on the principles of “Gross National Happiness” and 2) the Himalayan Buddhist temple, Tiger’s Nest which I’ve posted here. I’d seen photos of Tiger’s Nest for many years, but photos do not give you a sense of just how high up it is! 🌄📷 I’d had the impression that Tiger’s Nest was perched just above a city, and that you could look up and see it from a town below, sort of like the Potala Palace in Lhasa. That’s not the case - not even close! You’ll probably never see a photo of Tiger’s Nest from the valley floor on Instagram because it would be so boring—in a photo taken from the bottom, Tiger’s Nest would be just a tiny speck on the mountain side. 🗻For Americans or anyone who has been to Yosemite, imagine you’re standing on the valley floor and looking at the very tops of the highest rock surfaces and you see a small speck that *might* be manmade. That’s the best way I could relate to you how high up this special Bhutanese monastery is.  To visit the viewpoint from where I took this photo, you start at a forested valley floor, and hike up several hours. 🚶🏻🏃🏻‍♀️There’s no rock climbing involved, and its only steep in a few places, but the sheer length of the trek makes the existence of this place that much more remarkable. It’s not just its beauty and the seemingly impossible engineering that gives you a sense of awe,  it’s also the idea that every piece of wood, stone, every relic and jewel housed inside, was carried up one by one. 💪 Pro Tip: If you decided to visit yourself, start your journey before dawn, or in the afternoon, and you’re likely to have the viewpoint all to yourself. We did :) !! We were there so late, we came down in total darkness. Remember your flashlights.

Almost 11 weeks post explant and here is what I’ve learned about myself:

💗 I put them in at age 19 bc I didn’t feel good  about myself. I was self conscious THEN about being “flat” and that has not gone away. I had implants for 33 years and being a double DD became part of my identity. It feels stupid to admit that now but is true. Removing them has been more than a health thing. It’s been a deep dive into my own psychology and looking at why I felt I “needed them”

💗 I feel stronger than ever. PHYSICALLY. I’m grateful to have learned about the rupture as it’s amazing how many things in my body have normalized since they are out. My body is happier without them 

💗When I first removed them, I ordered a bunch of padded sports bras and bras.I wear NONE of the padded things now. I’m embracing the flat. I don’t care if “others” think it looks better not to- I’m done pretending to be something I’m not in my body.  I’m not even an A cup and it’s my way of apologizing to 19 year old me. I’m going to love and accept her  now the way she is.

💗I do notice big boooobs everywhere now. And YES I mourn mine some days. But more often than not, I’m grateful to have removed them and am embracing my new body. I do not regret explanting.

💗 It was not just the explant that healed me. I’ve done a LOT of deep gut work this last year and left a house that was covered with mold. So it was a combination. 

💗I used to think people that talked about BII were cray cray- now I think I was the crazy one. Why did I dismiss the possibility that implants could be harming me for so long 🙈 sooooo many people tried to tell me. I used to get triggered by that. 

💗 Alllllll my inflammation is GONE. So is my pain, my excess weight, my energy dips. I’m back to my familiar self.

Anyways- Hadn’t shared about my post explant thoughts in a while so thought I would!

RECETTE 🍪 

Cookies IG bas

Ingrédients secs :
👩‍🍳190g de poudre d’amandes
👩‍🍳1 càs de bicarbonate alimentaire 
👩‍🍳Une pincée de fleur de sel 
👩‍🍳120g de bon chocolat noir coupé en grosses pépites 
Ingrédients humides :
👩‍🍳2 càs d’huile de coco solide et juste ramollie, désodorisée 
👩‍🍳Quelques gouttes d’extrait de vanille 
👩‍🍳1 gros œuf
👩‍🍳2 càs de sirop d’agave

👩‍🍳Préchauffer le four à 190°C, mode chaleur tournante si possible.
👩‍🍳Couper au couteau les pépites de chocolat, afin.
👩‍🍳Dans un grand saladier, mélanger les ingrédients humides : battre énergiquement l’huile de coco ramollie avec le sirop d’agave au fouet. Ajouter l’oeuf, la vanille et fouetter bien.
👩‍🍳Dans un autre saladier, mélanger les ingrédients secs à la cuillère : poudre d’amandes et bicarbonate puis les 120g de pépites de chocolat et le sel.
👩‍🍳Verser les ingrédients secs sur les ingrédients humides et mélanger rapidement avec une cuillère à soupe ou une maryse, sans trop insister.
👩‍🍳Sur une plaque recouverte de papier sulfurisé, disposer des petites boules de pâte en les espaçant bien. 
👩‍🍳Enfourner pour 7 à 8 minutes à 190°C (selon la taille des cookies et le four). Pour moi, 7 minutes dans le four préchauffé pour 10 cookies. 

Bonne régalade 😋

CHANDELEUR 🥞

Crêpes IG bas

Ingrédients
🥞 150 g de farine intégrale de petit épeautre
🥞 300 g de lait d’avoine
🥞 2 œufs

Préparation
🥞 Dans un saladier, battez les œufs en omelette.
🥞 Délayez en versant 1/3 du lait.
🥞 Versez la farine dans le saladier et mélangez bien pour l’incorporer au mélange.
🥞 Ajouter progressivement le reste du lait, en fouettant bien avec la cuillère pour éviter les grumeaux.
🥞 Laissez reposer 30 minutes. 
🥞 Faites chauffer une poêle antiadhésive avec un peu d’huile de coco.
🥞 A l’aide d’une louche versez la pâte et répartissez dans la poêle. Faîtes cuire les crêpes de chaque côté quelques minutes.

Bonne régalade 😋

PETITE GOURMANDISE 😋

Macaron chocolat 
👩‍🍳150 g de sucre glace
👩‍🍳90 g de poudre d’amande
👩‍🍳15 g de cacao en poudre
👩‍🍳2 blancs d’oeufs moyens ou 3 petits (75 g en tout)
👩‍🍳10 g de sucre (glace ou normal)
👩‍🍳100 g de chocolat noir à pâtisser
👩‍🍳10 cl de crème liquide
👩‍🍳20 g de beurre

👩‍🍳Tamisez plusieurs fois le sucre, le cacao et la poudre d’amande pour obtenir un mélange très fin.
👩‍🍳Montez les blancs en neige très ferme. Lorsqu’ils commencent à être fermes, ajouter le sucre glace (les 10 grammes), en 2 fois.
👩‍🍳Ajoutez les blancs à la poudre (cacao/amande/sucre) et mélangez pour obtenir une pâte lisse, brillante.
👩‍🍳A l’aide d’une poche à douille, réalisez des petits cercles sur une feuille de papier sulfurisé ou une plaque de silicone.
👩‍🍳Laissez “pocher” à l’air libre 20 minutes.
👩‍🍳Préchauffez le four a 150°C.
👩‍🍳Enfournez les macarons 20 minutes (15 min si ce sont des petits macarons).
👩‍🍳Réalisez la ganache en faisant chauffer la crème et en la versant sur le chocolat en morceaux. Mixer, puis rajouter le beurre, mixer à nouveau et réserver au frais.
👩‍🍳Sortez les macarons, laissez-les refroidir quelques minutes, décollez-les et garnissez-les.

A little monday morning motivation. I loved this sound clip when I heard it. We can apply it to so many things…asking for help as a parent, going after what you want in your career or diving deeper in your relationship. Taking that step to move forward and get out of a rut… the list can go and on. I think we’ve all have had trouble with doing one or all of these things at some point in our lives.
✨
With each step forward or heck, within any moment of self doubt, I find myself reflecting on the last year, or five years or ten years and realizing how much growth I’ve experienced as an individual. It can be hard for many of us to see it at times, but if we look, it’s there. 

Rob and I were just talking about this the other night after we put our 3 year old to bed. 3 year old?! Wait…almost 4 year old…what?!? We’re coming up on 10 years of marriage and never did we think we’d be in Arizona with a toddler, build a house or have traveled to all the places we have. None of this was the plan ten years ago sitting on a beach during our honeymoon. There never really was a plan, but every step we took, it felt like a step towards a more authentic self. A step towards a happier, more flexible life, creating space to explore and love and learn and stumble unapologetically. We created that space for ourselves together as a couple and still continue to grow and learn. Now we get to create that as parents together for a special little human who makes us feel more than we ever thought we could. 
🧡
This is turning into a novel and I’m writing this out at night (to post in the morning) which is probably why i feel all the feels…but all this to say, I love these words and I think it’s the encouragement we need to remind ourselves and our loved ones to go after what we want …create the type of life that brings our souls that much closer to feeling full. 🙌

Simplicity, slowing down and creating intimate moments at home. Looking back it’s the quieter days that hold the most special memories with my family vs the big parties or grand trips. 

Many of us have our days filled with appointments, time to get from here to there, pick up this and that… we end up yearning for those slower moments but then are also programmed to think and feel it’s “boring” if we’re not constantly on the move. 🤔 

Why not make those times at home beautiful? Turn ordinary moments into extraordinary…just by switching our mind set…just by looking a little deeper and enjoying the beauty in the simplicity. 

I remember one summer as a kid, the AC went out for a good portion of the season. It was hot and humid (back east where I grew up.) My mom hung pretty sheets in the hallway to direct the airflow of the portable fan we had plugged in. My sisters and I gathered around with snacks and movies. I still remember the shadows dancing in our room, as we lowered the curtains to keep the heat from the sun out a bit. It felt magical and special, even though yes, we were hot…but we weren’t  focused on that at the time…

It’s easy to romanticize everyday moments if we let ourselves see things that way….a little more childlike, find some beauty and magic in it all…

3 reasons why I love working with silhouettes and you should too!

Emotional Resonance:
Silhouettes paint with emotions, casting a spell of drama and mystery. The strong contrast between darkness and light breathes life into my creations, conveying intense feelings that linger in the viewer’s soul.

Sculpting with Shadows:
In the world of silhouettes, details fade away, leaving room for the dance of form and composition. As an artist, I revel in the opportunity to sculpt with shadows, experimenting with angles, framing, and negative space to weave a visual tapestry that captivates the observer.

Universal Poetry:
Silhouettes are my universal language. They transcend genres and settings, allowing me to tell stories through shapes. From the quiet grace of a solitary tree to the silhouette of a cat, each frame is a canvas for my emotions, a testament to the versatility and timeless allure of this artistic expression.

“You can’t look at one of these and not wonder what’s going on with them,” said visual ecologist Katie Thomas. (@katiethomaskt)

Dr. Katie went into Sherlock Holmes mode when she first set eyes on this squid!

She binged watched 30 years of underwater videos @mbari_news collected which documented over 150 sightings of this squid & after close inspection, she noticed something really cool

This glittery deep-sea squid floats with its head down & fins up, sporting an enormous yellow eye that faces the water’s surface & a smaller eye directed toward the sea floor

Here’s why:

In the deep sea, it’s dark, almost like permanent nighttime! The big eye helps the squid catch even the tiniest bit of light that filters down from the sun or moon above.

The giant eye is on the hunt for the silhouettes of prey swimming above.

Some animals in the deep sea use a sneaky trick called counter-illumination, where they produce light from their bodies to blend in with the light from above. The squid’s big eye is adapted to see through this disguise and spot these hidden snacks! 🦑

But why is the big eye yellow? Well it turns out yellow filters out certain wavelengths of light, particularly blue light, which is most common in the deep ocean 🌊

This filtering can increase contrast & help the squid to better distinguish shapes and movements in the blue-dominated underwater environment.

Fun fact: Athletes wear yellow lenses because they’ve been shown to have a brightening effect in low-light situations due to their ability to reduce light scatter. They also increase the eyes ability to focus clearly 👁️ Whelp…GUESS WHAT ATHLETES, Squids already figured this out millions of years ago.

Growing BIG ol’ eyes is a luxury in the squid world, & nature doesn’t like to waste! So, the strawberry squid is super smart with its eye size—big where it helps, small where it can save on the squid-nergy bill! Talk about eye-economical!😂

Clownfish live in social groups with a strict hierarchy led by a dominant female — and in the absence of the dominant female, the largest male undergoes a sex change and becomes the new female. #DidYouKnow Clownfish are hermaphrodites, meaning they contain both male and female reproductive organs. In fact, when clownfish hatch from their eggs, all of them are born male. Out of the freshly laid group, the largest fish will become the dominant female. The second largest fish will become the dominant male. If the dominant female dies within the school of fish, the dominant male will then switch sexes and become the dominant female!

Part of my upcoming story on Zoroastrianism, the oldest monotheistic religion in the world, for @natgeo. Mehernosh, a pallbearer - the person in charge of carrying the dead body at a funeral - walks away from one of the two functioning towers of silence in Karachi.
A tower of silence, known as dakhma, is a circular structure built by Zoroastrians for excarnation - that means the exposure of human corpses to the elements for decomposition - in order to avoid contamination of the soil and other natural elements by the decomposing dead bodies. Carrion birds, usually vultures (though no longer in Karachi…) and other scavengers, consume the flesh. Skeletal remains are gathered into a central pit where further weathering and continued breakdown occurs. In this dakhma, reflective mirrors have been fitted inside the tower of silence to increase the heat and help the body decomposing faster.
Karachi, a city of 20 millions, has 800 Zoroastrians known as Parsees, 70% of them are above the age of 70 years old. #zoroastrianism #zoroastrian #towerofsilence #towersofsilence #parsi #parsee

I was in the dust with the wrestlers and I looked up and realised that a crowd had formed, a sea of shalwar kamiz. All these men (and 1 woman!! Can you spot her??) had gathered on the edge of a pilgrimage site to watch a spontaneous wrestling match - called Koshti or Malakhro in Baloch. With laughter and agitation, some theatre, it’s the ancestral raw version of the WWF stuff you might have unfortunately seen on TV. Pakistan, Baluchistan province.

I was in Karachi last March, city of 20 million, I love it there. On my pilgrimage in Baluchistan, I met a man who called himself Samundar Baba (Ocean Baba) - he owned boats. Unusual character, long beard and serious looking type, a big hashish smoker. He lived in Lyari, considered a dodgy area although I didn’t think so. I reached out and we met in his house. I was interested in this world of men you can find on fishing boats. So I asked him to bring me. This is the Korangi fishing harbor, one of the largest one in south asia. It can be complicated to photograph there because of authorisation and army nearby. Samundar kindly got me in and I spent a few hours jumping boats as the sun got low.

The original ravers were just getting started. Fun and mad times with the passionate Ishk Ali and his buddies, like Daula Sain. It was day 2 of our 12 days pilgrimage journey, walking together across Sindh and Baluchistan. That is a double cigarette and a sacrificial goat. Pakistan.

2023 is gone, just a number! It’s been a year filled with travels in Pakistan, Uzbekistan, Spain, Azerbaijan, Canada, Tajikistan, India etc…
It was interesting to meander through life between being a photographer, a farmer and be present for the family.
I thought of god a bit, all triggered by a story on Zoroastrianism for National Geographic magazine (coming up). How and why do we often inherit the feeling of being watched by God, god like a massive cctv system… religion the opium of the people?
Probably god is busy with a lot more than watching you… Is your god a vengeful one or a god that you will live with and whose law you must respect, like gravity? Lots of fun questions with no real need for answers..

Here is a serene scene, mixing all religious influences (at least to my eye!), in a place that has seen Animism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism and more recently Islam (ismaili faith). It’s in an “ostone”, a shrine in Tajikistan’s Wakhan corridor, adorned with ibex and Marco Polo horns - and a triangle of stones for the “shirogh” (the candle of cotton dipped in oil), lit for special occasion (for Jumarat, Eid or for Didor, the birthday of the Aga Khan etc). Azom Khon, the caretaker, is praying for me before I leave. It was beautiful so I pulled back and took a picture.

I will be sharing pictures here from my recent travels until I leave for SE Asia on February 20th.
Love and light for 2024.

Here, an all-woman ceremony beneath a hand-embroidered suzani marks a son’s departure to study in the capital, Tashkent. CREPES RECIPE!!! 🥞👨‍🍳🧑‍🍳Next Sunday is chandeleur in France 🇫🇷 meaning we’re gonna stuff ourselves with crepes all day long!! 😃These delicious crepes are filled with fried apples and bananas, coconut yogurt blended with blueberries, coconut caramel… Heaven!! 😋
So the crepe recipe is SUPER SIMPLE, 🤟I’ve been making it since forever, it’s my go-to basic and I love that it has 5 ingredients only, 👍 you know when a recipe says it’s super simple and the ingredients are beyond 6 or 7 you should definitely have your doubts hehe! 🧐 So no fancy flour, or exotic ingredients, or whatever here!!! Na-aaahhh! 😝 Just the basic that anyone has in the pantry. Also gotta say that : the first crepe you’ll make is always a flop, well at least this always happens with me! 🤷‍♀️ Who else has this problem??? 🤪 So don’t stop right there, make another one, everything will be fine! 🙌 Enjoy!!
✨
Ingredients
* 1 cup soymilk (or plant milk of your choice)
* 1 cup flour (can be a GF flour too)
* 3 tbsp cane sugar
* 1/2 tsp baking powder
* 1 tbsp coconut oil, melted
✨
Method
1. Put your flour in a bowl and form a well in the middle
2. Add cane sugar, melted coconut oil and baking powder
3. Whisk together adding the plantmilk little by little. Batter consistency should be very slightly thick
4. Heat a non-stick pan at medium heat, lightly oiled. Add a ladle and distribute evenly, to form a nice circle wait till it’s cooked (about 1 minute) and flip back on the other side. Allow the crepe to cook another 30 seconds to 1 minute before removing the crepe and placing it on a plate. Continue this process until all of the batter has been used.

A group of southern right whales draw closer to a tiny @mitty off the shores of Western Australia. Said to be called right whales for being the “right whale to hunt,” these gentle giants were once heavily targeted by the whaling industry. Their high fat and oil content, coupled with their tendency to stay close to shore, move slowly, and float after being harpooned, tragically made them the ideal victim for whalers. Since the global moratorium on whaling was officially established in the 1980s, their populations have slowly started to recover. As long as we continue to protect key calving and breeding grounds, mothers can raise their newborns in peace. We are very proud and grateful to work with our @sealegacy team to help ensure their future.

Visit the link in my bio to sign up for my next newsletter and find out how we can help our ocean’s giants thrive. With @mitty, @scott.portelli, @jaimenhudson, @_bugdreamer_, @rosie.leaney.

Tucked against the rocky coast, mother southern right whales find solace off of Western Australia. The protected shallows allow them to raise their newborns away from the threat of predators and speeding ships. Many people see the ocean as some muffled and infinite void, unaware that the constant din of boat traffic and mining the sea floor is virtually inescapable to an animal as sensitive as a whale. The more spaces they have to nurture their calves in peace, the more their species can recover.

In an incredible win for our ocean, the government of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands have announced a major expansion to the region’s marine protected area. In the wake of a recent @sealegacy campaign with @pewenvironment, Great Blue Ocean, and Blue Nature Alliance, the government is moving forward with extending their no-take zone, officially safeguarding 449,000 sq km of the surrounding waters. The first few years of a bear cub’s life are filled with uncertainty as they learn to navigate an often unforgiving environment. Winters can be long and brutal, which means they must gorge throughout the warmer months before settling into dens. And while the seasonal salmon runs provide much-needed protein for outlasting the cold, the rivers can quickly become crowded with large males who tend to guard the best fishing spots. However, grizzly cubs have one advantage when it comes to survival; the fierce and unconditional love of their mothers. As long as there is healthy wilderness for bears to roam in peace, siblings like this pair may grow and thrive under mom’s protection.

You look out on the horizon, when a spontaneous mist in the distance catches your eye. You squint and scan the vast, sparkling surface waters, lean in, and become captivated by the possibility of witnessing one of our ocean’s great giants. Then, you spot them– another signaling plume followed by the curl of their dorsal ridge, as the magnificent fluke trails behind.

As the whale retreats to its underwater kingdom, you’re left mesmerized, and curious of what lies ahead for them on their journey. Where are they headed? What does their world look like when they slip below the horizon?

On today’s #WorldWhaleDay, we celebrate these astounding creatures and the way they never fail to draw our attention out past the break and down into our ocean’s bustling ecosystems. When we allow the whale to guide our curiosity and accept their invitation to explore what lies beneath the surface, we’re welcomed by the knowledge of their compounding impact, and find our gratefulness for their presence only grows.

One of the advantages of spending weeks at sea and diving nearly every day is getting to see new sides to familiar wildlife. Just off the shores of The Bahamas, our team came across this bottlenose dolphin crater feeding, a hunting strategy named for the cavities left scattered across the ocean floor. After using echolocation to spot fish hiding deep in the soft sand, the dolphins dive in with their snouts, sometimes down to their pectoral fins, before wriggling back out moments later with their catch. Currently @Mitty and I are preparing to return to life aboard the SeaLegacy 1 and get back to working directly on the conservation front lines — starting in New Zealand. 4. Swim under the waterfall „Cascata do Poço do Bacalhau“ 💦

7. Explore the nature at „Miradouro da Ponta do Sossego“ 🌺
8. Book a whale watching tour - you will most likely also see dolphins 🐬 
9. Do the hike to the waterfalls „Poco da Ribeira do Ferreiro“ 👟
10. Visit the view point „Miradouro do Portal“ 🌊

1. Nagelhaut zurückschieben

5. Abfeilen 
6. 60 Sek. aushärten

I finished my 4 day trip to Austria and it's surely been nothing less than surreal. Being at the places which I just saw in mobile wallpapers, even when I was staring at the structures, I wasn't able to believe if this was actually happening. As I walked through, I tried to absorb every sight, every curve on the building, every turn of the road, every small piece of it made me realize why I love to travel. Entering random streets, talking to locals, navigating through public transport, shopping through local groceries, trying to live the culture that has been passed on over the years to form the country what it is today. It's much more than just fancy pictures, these reels or my lame stories I've been spamming with, it's breathing this air and being here. I'd be travelling to four more places on this trip and I don't know which one I would find the best, but this surely made a place in my heart.

For those who have lost something this week; an opportunity, a relationship, a belief, a job, faith or motivation...your next season is going to be greater!
-
What no longer serves you will eventually be cut, pruned or trimmed away from your life.
-
This hurts in the moment. That moment can last from minutes to months. And that’s entirely upto you. Own it, experience it, feel it.
-
Then there becomes a time when new life starts growing from the very area of your life that has been removed. New life that holds the promise of new opportunities, new memories, new relationships, new jobs and a renewed faith and motivation.
-
A word for anyone going through this right now...your next season is going to take further than your last one.
-
God never removes unless there is something far greater He has planned for our next season. The pruning is just the first step of new opportunities!
-
Believe in the hope of tomorrow, while you experience whole-heartedly and learn from today.
-
Your next season is going to be greater than your last. Have faith in knowing God will replace.

“I know I’m a handful baby”, part of the new series “Relationship status:”, where we (@wheresaddie and @aialahernando) use self portraiture as a means of translating/exploring the private as public female experience. 
The artists use site specific real floral arrangements, alongside contemporary artifacts within the artists’ lived experiences; the personal objects strewn across the works serve both as a portrait of the modern women but also of the artists themselves, to create a feeling of longing in the work- to see what is concealed, to understand who is attached. This form of active looking implicates the viewer into the process and highlights further into the series, the role of desire as a (un)productive force.

10 years ago today I bought my first camera. 
I was 24 at the time, finishing my second degree in Biotechnologies. 
Didn’t know anything about photography, didn’t have any connection or any real reason to start, out of the simple, uncontrollable need to express myself. 
I started so many things trying to find my way, always ending into dropping the latest idea after some months. 
Photography hit me like a bolt and never left me. 
Of all the things I heard during these 10 years, the most important one that kept pushing me in improving over and over again, was probably this: “you can’t”.
You can’t live with photography, you can don’t it without connections, you can’t work without expensive gear, you can’t make it without a specific degree, you can’t work with this “style”, you can’t do it because you’re not good enough. 
After 10 years at 34 years old, after years of absolute dedication and an insane will to improve still pumping in my veins, I’m living with photography the best life I could have imagined. 
I’m so grateful to all the people that believed in me and helped me trough this process; of course believing in yourself is the most important part, but without all the persons I met, I don’t know if I would have been able to make it trough the hardest times. 
This is just a small selection of some fav pictures shot during these years. 
I didn’t include the FaceTime series, even tho is probably one of the biggest steps for me in terms of improving my vision. 
Thanks to all the people involved, hope we’re gonna be able to meet in person soon again, to create, have fun and keep inspiring each other. 
If you have any question about the making of any particular photo, or the process in general, I’d love to talk about it here in comments.

Hello,

If you don’t know who I am, allow me to introduce myself. I’m Alex, I’m French but I grew up in Madrid, and I’ve been creating with a camera since 2009. “Professionally” since 2012. 

What gets me out of bed every morning is the deep desire to connect with people and environments. Meeting people and seeing places for the first time is a bit of an addiction.

I make photographs for brands when they hire me. I also make films for them too. I’m known for shooting landscapes and outdoors sports like cycling and hiking. I’ve also built a few companies such as @stayandwander (creative agency) and @wildistco (online photography school). I take pride in sharing what I know about the world of photography and have spent the last five years doing that both online and offline on photography retreats. 

Becoming a photographer happened by accident. As soon as I moved from France to Quebec to finish my design studies I got totally drawn in by the boreal forest and the harsh winters. It was, and still is an endless source of inspiration and peace. 

I struggle with scheduling because I am interested in a lot of things. I also struggle to make the time to go shoot more outside. Also, I’m a pretty bad handyman. 

I know it is very timely to hate on this app and what it is becoming. Although I agree with a lot of it, I’m also immensely thankful for this app that has allowed me to meet thousands of people. Some of which have become friends for life. It has also changed my life by helping create a career path for me and drawing sizeable exposure to my work. That I’ll never forget. 

With that said, It’s up to us to make IG what we want it to be… So here are my commitments to you: 

1. To always tell you like it is
2. To share work I’m proud of
3. To help you if you’re trying to help yourself.. (continued in comments)

MORE GLUTES IN YOUR DEADLIFT 🍑 OR MORE HAMSTRINGS 🍖 Here’s how you get your aim right…

GLUTE FOCUSED DEADLIFT 🍑
This requires more STRETCH of the glute muscle to occur because more stretch = increased tension = more activation & work required to contract the muscles again. And more work = MORE GROWTH!
👉🏼 so what do you need to do? 
Increase the amount of knee bend and lower the hips more. This creates a deeper fold at the hips (and also less tension in the hamstring) increasing the recruitment of the glutes 👌🏼

HAMSTRING FOCUSED DEADLIFT 🍖
The same principle applies. You need to create more stretch & length in the hamstrings compared to the glutes.
👉🏼 so what do you need to do?
Less bend in the knees (bust still a slight bend 😉) and keep the hips higher as you lower the bar. 

🎥 WATCH MY FULL YT VIDEO FOR A DETAILED & VISUAL EXPLANATION ☺️ (link in stories)

It’s important to note that both muscle groups will be active in a deadlift, no matter which variation you do. This technique tip helps you shift more or less tension into each muscle group depending on what your training goals are 😎 Hope this helps! PILATES FOR RUNNERS 👟 If you’re a runner, sprinter, or even walker, you should be doing this!

Building strength in the glutes, stability in the hips & maintaining active feet is so important for efficient & injury free leg driven km’s (or miles!) 🏃🏽‍♀️💨

I’ve sped these videos up a little bit so remember to do each exercise slowly and with purpose!

TRY BEFORE RUNNING:
1-3 rounds depending how much time you have (the more often you do these, the better results you will get 💪🏼)

▪️1. CLAM SEQUENCE
x10 each side

- do all 3 exercises in a row, making sure you don’t collapse in the bottom ribcage between each exercise.
- keep the hips still (like there are in concrete) 

💥WORKS: Glute med & min - important for good lower body gait & hip stability

▪️ 2. SL TUCK CIRCLES
x10 each side

- keep belly button pulled in as you hold hips high & aim to keep hips still.

💥WORKS: Glute max, med & min / hip flexors / abs - helps build hip stability during leg movement

▪️3. SL EXTENDED RDL
x10 each side

- standing leg always has a slight bend
- fold at the hips & keep spine long (sit into standing leg a bit deeper)

💥WORKS: Glute max, med & min, quads, hip flexor - improves balance, hip stability & foot strength

▪️4. HIP HIKES
x10 each side

- move slowly & through full range on every rep (full up - full down)

💥WORKS: Glute med & min / obliques - improves hip stability & lower body gait

▪️5. FOOT SEQUENCE
x10 each side

Heel-Toe
- as you lean back pick up all 10 toes. Spread them as wide as you can as you roll foot forward then rise to toes.

Outdide-Inside
- slight bend in the knees & aim to find edges of your feet while spreading toes.

💥WORKS: Calves / Smaller foot muscles - important for good foot biomechanics and strength (our feet become weak as we are constantly in shoes!)

WALL ANGELS 👼🏼 These were an absolute game changer for my shoulder pain. No joke.

Mid last year I started getting shoulder pain in the back of my shoulder blade that really affected my arm movements over head (including handstands! ) 😩 My favourite! I battled with it for months and tried lots of different rehab exercises but THIS ONE was what changed everything for me.

I started doing 10 slow reps throughout the day. I made a rule: every time I passed the same wall in my house, I would do 10 reps. Or when I was waiting for food to cook in the kitchen etc. It maybe ended up being 4-6 times in the day (so ~50 reps every day). 

It didn’t really affect the flow of my day too much BUT it completely eradicated my shoulder pain! 😱 Not to mention, my ‘winging’ shoulder blades that I have battled with all my life, are slowly finding a better position sitting FLAT onto my back (at last!!! 🥺🥰)

👉🏼 I CAN NOT RECOMMEND THESE ENOUGH. 👈🏼

Especially if you suffer from any upper thoracic pain, neck pain, back pain, poor shoulder movement, or struggle with bad posture.

⏰ As always, daily consistency will get you the best and quickest results. I still do these, but they are now a quick part of my warm up before any workout. It maybe takes 2 min to do 3 slow sets 👊🏼

Try it and let me know how you go! 👇🏼

Kenya is establishing a vital breeding population of 21 EASTERN BLACK RHINOS rhinos at @Loisaba_Conservancy in Laikipia, Kenya, where they have been absent for the past half-century. Moving a black rhino, an animal weighing over a ton, is a Herculean challenge fraught with danger at every turn. It begins with the risky task of sedating the massive creature, a procedure that requires precision and caution to ensure both the rhino’s safety and that of the vets and handlers. Once subdued, the real test begins as the sedated rhino must be carefully revived and maneuvered into a sturdy crate, a task made all the more daunting by the animal’s immense size and strength. Every step of this delicate operation underscores the inherent risks involved. Watch the sheer force of these creatures and imagine doing it over 21 times over the course of 2 weeks. The teams from @kenyawildlifeservice executed the operation with unparalleled expertise and dedication. In an ideal world, we wouldn’t have to go through these extreme measures but with approximately 80% of the world’s remaining eastern black rhinos under its protection, Kenya’s efforts offer a glimmer of hope for the future of these magnificent creatures.

I am humbled to share another remarkable conservation story from Kenya: the resurgence of eastern black rhinos from the brink of extinction. In a pivotal moment, Kenya is reclaiming its role as a haven for these creatures, establishing a vital breeding population at @Loisaba_Conservancy in Laikipia, Kenya, where they have been absent for the past half-century mainly due to poaching and long ago,  trophy hunting. This first image shows the moment a rhino was resuscitated after it stopped breathing and quickly released. The arduous tasks of tracking, darting, and relocating 21 of these critically endangered giants, each weighing over a ton, posed formidable challenges, yet the teams from @kenyawildlifeservice executed the operation with unparalleled expertise and dedication. Their efforts offer a glimmer of hope for the future of these magnificent creatures. The final image shows the skull of the last rhino poached in the 1970s resting beneath a celestial canopy, symbolizing this hopeful shift as Kenya now stands  as a nation that is expanding habitat and bolstering rhino populations. With approximately 80% of the world's remaining eastern black rhinos under its protection, Kenya is safeguarding endangered populations for future generations. 

I want to sincerely thank all the partners and encourage you to follow @nature_africa @nature_org @loisaba_conservancy  @kenyawildlifeservice  @olpejeta @sandiegozoo @spaceforgiants  @elewanacollection @lewaconservancy

An international team of scientists and conservationists achieved a groundbreaking milestone in their mission to save northern white rhinos from extinction. They successfully conducted an in vitro embryo transplant in a southern white rhino, resulting in a pregnancy—a crucial proof of concept. However, the joy was short-lived as unforeseen tragedy struck due to heavy rainfall and flooding, unearthing Clostridia bacteria spores and leading to a devastating infection that claimed both the mother, Curra, and the 70 day old fetus.

Despite this profound loss, the team remains determined, having worked tirelessly for years to create 30 embryos with Avantea lab. This awe-inspiring creature was a 70-day-old rhinoceros fetus, an embodiment of perfection in its miniature form. While a typical southern white rhino can tip the scales between 3,080 and 7,920 pounds and 11-15 feet, this little one only reached a delicate 6.4 inches. His life was cut short when his surrogate mother, Curra, a southern white rhino, succumbed to an unforeseen tragedy triggered by heavy rainfall and flooding that unearthed Clostridia bacteria spores, leading to a swift and devastating infection.

The news of Curra's demise struck the team with profound grief. These dedicated individuals have been tirelessly working for years to rescue the northern white rhinos from the brink of extinction. Their journey brought them to Kenya, where they were on the verge of confirming the success of creating the world's first rhino pregnancy through embryo transfer at the Ol Pejeta Conservancy. In a bittersweet twist of fate, the entire team received word of the successful pregnancy by implantation of an embryo using in vitro fertilization (IVF). However, this moment of joy was tinged with the somber acknowledgment of the journey's cost. The next pivotal step is to transfer northern white rhino embryos into a surrogate mother.

I'll be sharing more of this extraordinary story in the coming weeks.  Stay connected with the @biorescue_project, @safariparkdvurkralove, @leibnizizw, @olpejeta, #avantea, and @kenyawildlifeservice for more insights into this pivotal moment for northern white rhinos.

From playful antics to tender moments, elephants flow with emotion. While the calves at Reteti Elephant Sanctuary (@r.e.s.c.u.e) have traumatic pasts, the love and companionship of the other elephants and the dedicated keepers help them grow and heal.

FROM MY ARCHIVE | Monhegan Island Post 05 (final):: I got my start at @natgeo in 1999 as a photo intern when I did my first story for the magazine. I was asked if I had an idea for a project and I proposed Monhegan – a small island 10 miles off the coast of Maine. I am from New England and had lived on the Maine coast as a young adult. I had always been curious about the 2 mile long and ½ mile wide island. In the summers the place overflows with tourists, but the year round population is only about 60-70. The islanders’ de facto fishing territory became the Monhegan Lobster Conservation Area in 1996 with a limited season starting in October. The island’s windswept landscape, quirky community and the dramatic cliffs have inspired artists like Robert Henri, George Bellows, Rockwell Kent, Edward Hopper, Lynn Mapp Drexler and three generations of the Wyeth family to name a few. ⁠
⁠
The community took me in and sometimes chewed me up. My time and experiences there changed and shaped my life in profound and beautiful ways that continue to impact me almost 25 years later; working with photo editor Susan Welchman who took me under her wing and has been my mentor and dear friend since and within days of arriving to the island, I also met one of my best friends @tralice_pooltoyphotos ⁠

The way I see it, “Mobility” Is kind of like a collaboration effort between our muscles and joints.
 
When our joint mobility is limited, we might be missing out on opportunities to be stronger, more athletic, and more efficient.
 
The ability to move our joints through their full range helps our muscles work more optimally, and when our muscles can do their work, they can also get stronger and help keep our joints healthy in return.
 
💪🏼Having a good balance between strength and joint mobility helps distribute the stress more evenly through the body instead of overstressing our joints (back, hips, knees, ankles, etc.).
 
🚪Our joints are kind of like the hinges to a door; if that door remains unopened for long periods in addition to environmental decay, the hinges in that door will start creaking and get rusty overtime. In our case, it will be arthritis, bursitis, inflammation, and things like that.
 
So you see, just as with the door example, maintenance and movement were keys to extending the life and function of it, in our case, MAINTENANCE and MOVEMENT are also keys to a BETTER QUALITY OF LIFE.🙌🏼

STAY ACTIVE!💪🏼

- Amplified the role of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands to our global community while urging protections that would maintain the Southern Ocean’s stability.

Angkor Wat and park in Siem Reap, Cambodia. This is my second time here and it still feels as mystical as the first time. At the beginning of our tour, our guide overwhelmed us with all the mathematical calculations and engineering ingenuity that went into building Angkor Wat. Certain points of the structure lined up perfectly with the Draco Constellation and the sun positioning at sunset. Although there are educated speculation from experts archeologists saying this dates back about 900 years ago, It’s all a mystery.

On the other hand, Spiritual channelers have mentioned this to be older than 5000 BC. It’s a place to activate the pineal gland (third eye) through frequencies, it’s also an informational point for earth to funnel data to and from other planets/galaxies. It’s like another access point of information like the great pyramids. The art carvings hold a lot of relations to Hinduism on many of the Angkor Park structures. But personally, I see a lot of psychedelic reflections on some of the temples. They almost look like what I see as the crossover realm between the mind and other outer dimensions. It’s like the level where you have to overcome the ego before connecting with your higher self. Very interesting place to walk around and wander off into.

caption:
Make sure to save this info if you’re thinking about visiting Vietnam. We’re in Ben Tre, Vietnam and this has got to be one of the most underrated places we’ve learned about. I hope people keep going to Bali and leave this place for us 😆

This town is 2 hrs south of Saigon - which around $40 Grab ride.  The town itself is pretty developed as in roads and sidewalks, but this is where you can relax from the crazy traffic and roads of Saigon. I think Ben Tre fits the criteria of what many people think of Saigon. It’s a growing city, with no crazy developments, or high rise.  Many restaurants or stores here cater to the locals, so you will get more of an authentic experience. The locals are pretty friendly as long as you are respectful. The kids like to say “hello” to my bf because they want to use their English. They get a good chuckle when he says “hi” in Vietnamese. We usually greet and thanks in the language of the country we’re in, many folks seem to appreciate it.  The young locals speak English well, older people usually don’t. 

We did 3 tours here with @mrbikerbentreboattour , Troy found him on TripAdvisor. We highly recommend his tours. After doing our first private boat tour, we came back for another tour of the town, and then rented bikes from one of the eco lodges/homestays. @mrbikerbentreboattour has been extremely punctual and helpful with us. His tours gives you a sample of the local lifestyle and Vietnamese tradition. We’ve got to visit the small canals off the Mekong river, and private roads of the locals. We did not experienced any upsell, pressure to buy, or nonsense stops on the tours. It felt more educational and you can see the aunties and uncles on his team working diligently to make a good impression for us. We really appreciated our stay here. It’s so walkable around and the local people love coming out after the sun set but that’s when we are asleep 😴 #travelvietnam #bếntre

Ben Tre, Vietnam

Last year, I was in total hermit mode. I was so eager to build my homestead, I couldn’t focus on anything else. I think that is why I am walking everywhere I possibly can in Vietnam. However, today is a biking day! We rented some bikes at an eco homestay through @mrbikerbentreboattour and it was exactly what I needed. It was so much fun  going around the town on our bikes. There were so many fun fruit shops and Sugarcane juice stand. 🍺 We both got a delicious drink off one of the stands for 50 cents and it was absolutely divine! 
Also, I had one of the most amazing Banh Xeo of my life. We found a random farm that also runs a restaurant and they made us the most incredible Banh Xeo.  I’m already sad to think how much I will miss today 🥲 #vietnamtravel #bentre

Today we decided to check out a park in Saigon. Creating a little reference point gives us a little mission to embark on and get our steps in 😊 This is  always a nice way to discover small gems or see places you would not be able to read or watch about. On our walkie walk, we were able to see the contrast in the city. One of my pics shows the old way of living off a stream (how my parents described their life growing up), and behind it are the new skyscrapers. 

As we walked, we discovered more street foods, mini restaurants, and cafes. I got some sugarcane juice off an auntie from a side stall and then stumbled into a little oasis off a super busy bustling road. It was a little coffee stale with lots of unique and local plants surrounding it. Great place for coffee and plant enthusiasts 🪴 There were little tables and seats hidden around an array of hanging plants. Later I found out it was a plant shop too! This was a nice little break stop for another refresher. Troy got his iced coffee and so we got to sit amongst all these pretty greenery. Everything is such a contrast in Saigon. You see old vs new everywhere, the crazy busy hustle of traffic, and Vietnamese taking their naps in the mist of all the chaos in the streets. I really enjoy observing 👀 and wondering how people adapt to the places they live in.

My Barbie moment at a super pink church in Saigon! It’s incredibly hot here but I heard it’s -25 back home, so we’re not complaining! I’ll take this heat and over stimulated city for the time being 🧡 

I thought that crowded places gives me anxiety but what I learned is that the environment and people affect me. Crowded places don’t give me anxiety, the collective energy of the same things do. Sometimes my environment can feel like a drag. People talking about the same things, focused on career, status, gossip, politics, limited beliefs, problems after problems. And when I’m around it too much, it sucks the life force out of me, so I retract. Exploring helps me break free from that. Any sort of traveling, mini trips, or taking off on a plane helps me break free from monotony and repetition. Walking in places is also very grounding for me. I’ve noticed that I need a balance of both worlds, the chaotic city and being in nature. When I become extreme in one, I definitely can feel the lack of balance in my overall energy. We are all different and I’m learning more on how to listen to my personal inner guide. #saigon #vietnam

Anthony Bourdain made a lot of videos  in Vietnam. He definitely created a pathway for international foodies to embrace it’s unique culture. A lot has changed here in development but some of his recommended stops are still around. This place specializes on one of my favorite dishes, Banh Xeo! Banh Xeo looks like an omelette; but it’s not, it’s rice flour, turmeric gives it the yellow color, some people add coconut milk, and beer to the batter making the outer crepe shell crispy. Snippets from the woodworking studio with Yoshida-san @monkeyhold_japan in 大垣 (Ogaki), Japan over the summer. 

Shaping these holds was a lesson in allowing the medium lead to the final form rather than having the mind dictate the outcome. The practice was about inhibiting the urge to mold the wood into a shape I had pre-envisioned; instead, surrendering to the wood, imagining how best to reveal its beauty and unique form. 

To hold something is gratifying, but the more I climb, the more curious I become about the entire ecosystem that holds the boulders. When examined more closely, the 侘寂 of the wood is unveiled through the imperfections of the gnarled knots, the layers and swirls of age lines that hold the stories of the tree the wood came from 🤍 🌳

🌱I’ve been fascinated by this form of textile art for quite some time but never took the initiative to experiment w it till this year. In a conversation w my mom about folk art in Japan, the topic of this ancient method of manual resist dying came up and her eyes instantly sparkled with excitement as she shared her story of working with dye in her youth. As a child to immigrant parents who are reserved in speaking of their past, i have a hazy idea of what they were like in their youth and the environment in which they grew up in. Anyways, I love how shibori became a catalyst to paint a more vivid picture of my mom’s past 🌿It felt extra special to learn some shibori techniques from my mom with dear friends💖 

Some quotes I love from master dyer Fukumi Shimura: 

“I have received color without limit from the natural world in the years since I entered the dyer’s way. It has poured down on me endlessly, too much for this meager vessel to hold. Joyful as a child with a new set of paints, I have woven and woven yarn dyed by the grasses and trees”. 

“I don’t tell the acorn or gardenia seed pod or plum bar what color I want – I listen to the voice of the plants.” 

Hope I get the chance to practice and learn from the shibori masters in Japan soon 🎨

Malibu is also a word of Chumash origin, which is the name given to groups of California Indians that lived around the south-central coast. Chumash is derived from Tcú-mac, a word used by the Coastal Chumash to refer to Santa Rosa Island natives. Before the Spanish arrived, Chumash natives lived along the coast from San Luis Obispo to Malibu Canyon, and as far east as the edge of San Joaquin Valley.

One of the things I’m most thankful for is the ability to explore West Coast nature, like this spot: Malibu Tunnels⛰🕳

It’s a windy channel of conglomerate rock that acts like a barrier from the turbulence of civilization. There’s a canopy of cottonwoods and live oaks scattered about. Rattlers basking in the sun. A honeycomb mounted in a hueco. A flow of creek water cascades down and through the rock piles. Further down the stream, a face of cobblestone rocks- purple, green, brown, red- protruding upon a beige sandy looking canvas.

There’s a busy road a hundred feet above; honking and roadside noise remind us that this respite is in close proximity to a bustling city. But then the gurgling water overwhelms the sound of motor vehicles emanating from above, dislodging you from the constraints of spatial and temporal associations, you can almost close your eyes and forget where you are.

- You are your own best friend , respect and love on yourself harder than anyone else

- The universe has got your back , really know everything will be ok and tough times create tough humans and you will always come out stronger.
- Victim mentality achieves nothing , but sometimes you are a victim to certain situations and it’s ok to have feelings around those times.

I type this 1st log entry from Barcelona - ~ 2.000 Km into our 8.000 #iberitron road trip
.
Short summary how things went down till now:
* Austria is HPC heaven - except in Villach (see the drama in @audidriven story iberitron 02)
* Italy is getting better - although after our 3rd visit to @ionity.official Portogruaro - this location is definitely a dump (stinking trash containers next to the chargers, littering, not appealing at all
* @ionity.official France has a serious problem (1st station 4 stalls: 1 of 4 working = 1 broken - where I parked 1st, 2nd working - where I reparked, 3&4 only charging with ~35kW / 2nd station 6 stalls: 2 out of six delivered the full speed (150kW for the e-tron), the other ~35kW. Again lucky as I got the 2nd working one after reparking) Got lucky
* Spain 🇪🇸 - a little to early to tell but was already pleasantly surprised, as proven by this picture. In the middle of nowhere - Figueres - I found this working (!) HPC charger. Biggest challenge was to get the operator app working as it does not accept any of the charging cards
* A general not surprising rule: try to always charge before the night (like in this case) or even better over night as currently in our Barcelona hotel. For me the charging stops are part of the adventure (now locations, new experiences) but apparently my family thinks differently 😂. Yesterday we had zero charging stops (“boring” for me, enjoyable for family)
.
When we arrive at my moms place near Malaga I will try to do a more detailed day by day posts if desired 😉

Adm Elektrik, Aydın Söke’de başlattığı ‘Leyleklere Yeni Yuva’ projesi ile doğal yaşamın sürdürülebilirliğine 14 yıldır destek oluyor. Elektrik direklerine özel platformlar kurarak leyleklere güvenli yuva alanları sağlamak, göç dönemlerinde yuvaları kontrol ederek zararlı maddeleri temizlemek ve elektrik hatlarını yalıtarak leyleklerin güvenliğini sağlamak gibi adımlar atarak, hem doğal dengeyi koruma hem de leyleklerin yaşam alanlarını güvence altına alma konusunda çok değerli bir rol üstlenmişler. 
Boyle  çevre dostu projeler, içimizi ısıtan bir umut ışığı gibi parlıyor. “Leyleklere Yeni Yuva” gibi projeler, yalnızca doğal yaşamı değil, dünyamızın daha yaşanabilir olacağına dair  umutları da besliyor

Pre & post menopause has been a rollercoaster! I’m 49, and I’ve been navigating this ride for the past 9 years. (Peri menopause started at age 40🫠)

One thing I forgot to mention in this video is that SLOW weight loss is the BEST kind of weight loss! There is no rush. Be consistent even if it takes years because the slower it comes off the better for long term success.

It’s taken me over 2 (maybe more) years to lose the belly fat. Before I get comments about how I looked great before and didn’t need to lose the weight… here’s the deal:

Visceral fat is fat around your organs & can lead to many health complications. When I started gaining weight around my belly, it wasn’t subcutaneous fat that you could pinch. It was hard, and felt so uncomfortable.

I knew that I had to figure out why this was happening or rather what I could do to stop & reverse the weight gain.

Spring in the quilted hills, and the perennial question. Where to go next, or perhaps better stated, how to grow next? I really enjoy the notion, that ideas are alive and independent, like butterflies flittering about. There’s two ways to catch ‘um. You can run yourself ragged chasing. Or you can chill and enlarge the net.

Wyoming has quickly become one of my favorite backpacking destinations. Two years ago I spent a week in the Wind River Range, then last summer I joined @elisabethontheroad as she documented our climb up Cloud Peak in the Bighorn Mountains for @visitwyoming

I’ve followed the work of plein air painters from this state before I ever picked up a camera. It’s been fun growing familiar with the language of the landscape first hand, to see the peaks and valleys that translated to such inspiration. 

Finding beauty can be straightforward, it shines unabashed, but exploring what you have to say about a place takes time. It may even be through the creative process itself that you discover it. I often learn as much during a week on the computer with a digital paintbrush, as a week on the trail. Wouldn’t trade the epiphanies provided by either.

If your curious about the specifics of our climb, you can find Elisabeth’s article at TravelWyoming.com. #ThatsWY #WYresponsibly
Exploring an idea. One-new, two-an update, three-from a few years back.

“Unlike Earth, the atmosphere of Mars is dominated by micron-size dust aerosols, and the sky during sunset takes on a bluish glow.” From: Applied Optics Vol. 53, Issue 9

I’ve been experimenting with the public domain images available on the NASA website. What you see here are constructed entirely from that source. It’s been strange, and wasn’t until I found the article referenced above that I realized why. The light on Mars is ‘weird’ because the atmosphere is different. Go figure.

As I worked, the project became as much about understanding this unique light as playing with Martin landforms. The images here explore a few ways to bridge a blue light source - with golden/orange scattering, across a few different angles and times of day in a variety of atmospheric dust. It’s definitely not accurate, and surely exaggerated. (Check out the article, lots of math above my ability) The science was simply a point of departure for experimentation. The main gist i held in mind, is that blue can transition through purple & red or green & yellow to get to orange. Just walk your way around a color wheel. Fun. After a month tho, I’m ready to go look at some foliage.

There’s a balance between surface and substance, the aesthetics of an image and its meaning. I tend to think craft is important, but offers diminishing returns. In contrast, the possibilities for conceptual exploration are endless. It’s the difference between learning a language and finding what you have to say with it.

My favorite time in art history was between the late 1800’s and the early 1900’s, when the method used to create something started gaining awareness of its contribution to content. An interest in the mechanics of light and sight created the dappled visual color mixing of the impressionists. An interest in the mechanics of time and space gave birth to the multiple overlaid perspectives of cubism. I keep thinking about this as I flew about the mountains, collecting images from multiple moments and perspective.

Does any of this matter to the viewer and the final? Maybe. There are plenty of images I’ve enjoyed for their ideas, and plenty for aesthetics alone. But on this side of the image, the one of discovery and creation, building something with a conceptual foundation makes all the difference between a meaningful process and a simply stylish one. It’s powerfully good to stay in touch with that little kid inside, who endlessly asks “why?!”

One of my favorite fascinations is searching for repeated patterns in scale, micro and macro. Maybe it has to do with searching for something fundamental in the nature of things, or maybe it’s just fun to pretend you’re giant or very very small. 

This digital painting came together with shots from the mavic3 while climbing, and macro shots of rocks collected along the way.

Matching light and atmosphere is the most important factor to make a realistic scene, but texture is one of the biggest scale giveaways, so drones are the perfect tool to marry the two. 

@DJIglobal #mavic3 #imageaboveeverything

Migratory interests. I’ve been taking a little break from pixel painting and posting,  exploring a few new fascinations.  Then last month, DJI asked me to try out their Mavic3. Always happy to see through a different lens, I spent a couple weeks dodging fall storms in Idaho. (Really digging the extended battery life BTW.) Ironically, I’m now realizing my artistic process; harmonizing an eclectic array of images (somewhere around 30 here), isn’t so different than life process; harmonizing an eclectic array of interests. I really think the key is remembering to identify with the fascination, not the subject of it. Trust that single source of light, and the rest will sort itself in time, or Photoshop.

The clam diggers. A rainy day conversation with, James Abbott McNeill Whistler, and Idris Khan, perhaps a drop in by Todd Hido...

I don’t know any of these cats. Idris and Todd are making powerful work today, but James was born in 1834, so it might be a challenge for us to get together. But, that’s the cool thing about art. We can dialogue with anyone throughout time.

This one finds me curious about their feelings on substance vs style. Inspiration vs appropriation. The relationship between how we make something, and why. 

Idris created a seminal series that appropriated the work of Bernd and Hilla Becher, with (it appears) the intent of adding meaning. Todd’s style is highly copied by other contemporary photographers, who arguably don’t add additional meaning. And James was a big proponent of art for aesthetics alone - meaning be damned (and fought over in lawsuits.) Of course his stance was taken in an age when images were relatively rare and filled with allegory, which to him might have made this fight feel - quite meaningful. 🙃

American badlands. 

There is freedom being an outsider, to see culture in memetic terms, languages modular and mutable. To identify, simply through that which you happen to be appreciating. Right now, there is blue sky and sunlight on the hills.

Rock arrangement in sea minor. I grew up on this beach, playing with toy boats, pretending boulders were islands. Things haven’t changed much. My fascination with scale is the same as it ever was. The large central rocks are actually just close up photos of the same stones from the beach. I built a small pool and arranged them separately in still water.

Some of my favorite experiences with art started in boredom or confusion, then - after learning about the ideas behind a work, continued in appreciation. How cool is it that we can dialogue with anyone throughout history by responding to them with a few ideas of our own.

This scene may just be a simple sunset (or a boring one), but in addition to memories and scale, here are a few of the random things I was musing on while working:

Six Persimmons - The classic Chinese painting by the Buddhist monk Muqi. (An image that’s taken me years to understand).

Zen gardens and stones - They’re often used as a cliche representation for dreamy, sleepy relaxation, spa treatments and the like, when the reality of Zen practice can be quite serious and ardent effort towards waking up. I’m fascinated by the popular culture misunderstandings, perhaps because I held them so long myself.

Music - Visual spacing and rhythm, horizontal bars and notes; the staccato feeling of eye movement related to musical spacing and rhythm and spacing and rhythm and spacing and rhythm.
This was too good not to shoot something extra.

This are images from an old project from 2002.
The project was born out of one of the most traumatic experiences I had as a journalist - and it is - in a way - the beginning of my career.

In the Summer of 2002 I traveled to Israel and the West Bank and Gaza - fresh out of school hoping to find my way into the industry. I did whatever naive kid did back then, and parachuted my way into a story that I had little nuanced appreciation for. 

In the midst of trying to document life in Hebron between the Jewish settlers and Palestinian residents, I was beaten by a mob of 20 Jewish settlers during a violent funeral/riot in the center of the city. Interestingly enough an Israeli soldier was also beaten by the settler mob. 

I lost all my photography equipment I had saved up for, driving the “drunk bus” route in school, and dislocated my shoulder, and fractured my elbow and knee.

My mentor at the time - James Colburn (the DC bureau photo editor for Time Magazine) told me I couldn’t leave. That if I left - “I would always be scared” 

So I stayed - and he shipped me some old Nikon F3s he had lying in his office.

I spent the next month looking for a different story, and I found it in the most cliche place - A mental institution.

There was an old geriatric wing of this psychiatric facility in Bethlehem. For patients from all over the country. The doctors said some were Jewish, some were Muslim, some were Christian. No one knew for sure, many had been dropped off as infants. The facility had originally been administered by German, then British, then TransJordanian, then Israel and at the time I was there - the Palestinian Authority. 

And it was filled with many patients. They were all psychologically damaged or impaired. But interestingly enough - they got along with each other.

They were insane. But at peace.
And everyone outside was sane, but waging war.

Makes you think about who is really in their right minds. 

#photojournalism #palestine #israel #reportage #documentary

One of the other projects I did in Yemen were these portraits of Yemenis that played into the assignment I was working on, along with people I met during wanderings around different cities. 

This project could be the indirect reason I was detailed when I came back to the US. 

The second image is a portrait of the leader (at the time) of Al Qaeda’s political wing in Yemen.  He really liked the image and asked if I could send it to him. We used the old “bump” iPhone app to exchange the image. And I’m pretty sure my phone was compromised from there on out. 

To make matters worse - we were meeting in a large cafe for safety - the next interview subject came in to meet the writer and I a bit early. The third image is a portrait of the last Rabbi in Yemen. Obviously the head of Al Qaeda and the Rabbi kept their affiliations on the DL - so neither knew who each one was. They actually exchanged pleasant greetings and traded places - as the rabbi stayed for an interview and portrait.

The fourth image is a former Guantanamo prisoner who was returned to Yemen after serving a few years in the prison and found either not guilty or not worth US efforts to interrogate him. He was unemployed and trying to figure out how to continue a life cut short.

This month marks 20 years since one of the most impactful moments of my life when a shark took my arm while on a surfing off the coast of Kauai, my birth place. Many people could look at the incident back in 2003 as a major setback for me, but God had so much in store for the future! 🤙🏼

It’s absolutely wild to think how my life started and where it is now and all the amazing yet challenging things in between. I didn’t wake up in the hospital thinking I was invincible and was gonna get back to surfing. After getting a hint of inspiration,  I had to dream it up, flip my mindset and be willing to do what I had not seen anyone else do.  This was a challenge to live in faith. And I am so glad I was willing to try and give it my best shot! 🙏🏼 Now I get to surf with my two eldest sons Tobias and Wesley and my hubby! I get to enjoy these sweet moments with my newborn daughter. There is so much to be grateful for, and these past 20 years have been filled with incredible moments and huge overcoming seasons. 💛

When you have your “Shark Attack” moments in life. I hope you’re willing to try, and give life your best shot! You too CAN OVERCOME!

Changing your mindset is free. Doesn’t mean it’s an easy or fast fix. It’s up to you to be honest with yourself and start working on it. 
It’s wild to me that some people still think surfing with one arm is not possible. I am a living example and there are soooo many other amazing adaptive athletes and people out there doing incredible things that people perceive as impossible. 
What is it about some who are willing to adapt and make the most of what they’ve got? 
MINDSET. It may take time to switch it up and we may have to be forever workin at it. But I promise you, that you won’t regret continually flipping your mind to be more grateful, more optimistic, more of what and how can can I do this life to the best of my abilities… More of - I don’t need easy I just need possible. 🧠✨💪🏽 Hope this pushes you today and onward to adapt in your life. YOU CAN.

We didn't know it at the time this photo was captured, but this special leopard – her eyes alive with curiosity and wonder – would have a massive impact on our lives and careers. This is Legadema, the star of our film Eye of the Leopard. We spent over three years filming and documenting her growth from wide-eyed cub to confident huntress. She let us into her secretive world and helped fuel our passion to protect Africa's threatened wild cats. Although Legadema is no longer with us, her legacy lives on. This #WorldWildlifeDay, we're reflecting on the special time we spent with her, and renewing our dedication to protect our planet's precious wild species and spaces.⁣
⁣

Battles between lions and buffaloes are unpredictable, brutal and intense. Adult male African buffaloes can weigh over 900 kilograms and they are notoriously belligerent. It takes careful coordination, acute timing and immense courage for lions to successfully hunt these massive animals. Often when the fight appears to be nearing its conclusion, a final show of strength from the buffalo – sometimes backed by the rest of the herd – can swing the odds in its favour. Sadly, for this bull, his resilience was overpowered and the lions succeeded.⁣
⁣⁣
